title: From Caterpillar to Butterfly
summary: How a butterfly changes from an egg to a caterpillar, a chrysalis, and a winged adult, and how butterflies feed, travel, and stay safe.
poll: A caterpillar and a butterfly are really the same animal.

versions.title: A Bug Grows Wings
versions.text:
See the tiny dot on the leaf? It is an egg. A butterfly laid it there.

The egg hatches. Out comes a caterpillar. It eats its egg shell first. Then it eats leaves. It eats and eats. It grows fast. Soon its skin is too tight. So it sheds the skin. A new skin is under it. It does this four or five times.

Then it hangs from a stem. It makes a hard case. The case is a chrysalis. In there, the old body breaks down. It turns to a kind of soup! Then a new body forms. This can take two weeks.

The case splits. Out comes a butterfly! Its wings are wet. It waits for them to dry. Then it can fly.

It does not chew. It sips nectar from flowers. It has a long tube. It works like a straw. It tastes with its feet! It moves pollen, too. That helps plants make seeds.

Some fly far. Painted ladies fly from Africa to Europe. They do it each year.

In Saudi Arabia, look for the plain tiger. It lays eggs on ushar. This plant has a bad juice. The young eat it. So birds do not like them.

versions.title: A Bug Grows Wings
versions.text:
Look under a leaf. Do you see a tiny round dot? It may be an egg. A butterfly laid it there with care.

When the egg hatches, out comes a small caterpillar. First it eats its own egg shell. Then it eats leaves, and it grows fast. Soon its skin gets too tight. So it sheds the skin. A new, big skin is under the old one. This can take place four or five times.

Then it stops eating. It hangs from a stem and makes a hard case. This case is called a chrysalis. Inside, the old body breaks down. It turns to a kind of soup! Then a new body forms. For lots of kinds, this takes two weeks.

At last the case splits. A butterfly comes out. Its wings are wet and soft. It pumps them out. Then it waits for them to dry so it can fly.

A butterfly does not chew. It sips nectar from flowers with a long tube like a straw. It can taste with its feet! As it sips, it moves pollen from flower to flower. That helps plants make seeds.

Some fly very far. Painted ladies go from Africa to Europe each year.

In Saudi Arabia, look for the plain tiger. It lays its eggs on a plant called ushar. The plant has a bad juice. The young eat it, so birds do not like their taste. Birds leave them be.

versions.title: From Caterpillar to Butterfly
versions.text:
Look closely under a green leaf. You might see a tiny round dot. It may be a butterfly egg. The mother chose that plant with care, since its leaves are the food her young will need.

When the egg hatches, a small caterpillar crawls out. Its first meal is often its own egg shell. Then it starts to eat leaves, and it grows very fast. But its skin can not stretch much. When the skin gets too tight, the caterpillar sheds it. A new, bigger skin is waiting under it. This takes place four or five times.

When it is fully grown, it stops eating. It hangs from a stem and forms a hard case. This case is called a chrysalis. Inside, something amazing happens. The old body breaks down into a kind of soup! Then the parts of a new body form. For many kinds, this takes about two weeks.

At last, the case splits open, and a butterfly climbs out. Its wings are wet and crumpled. It pumps them full and waits for them to dry. Then it can fly away.

A butterfly can not chew. It sips sweet nectar from flowers through a long tube that works like a straw. It can even taste with its feet! As it feeds, it brings pollen from flower to flower. This helps plants make seeds.

Some butterflies go very far. Painted ladies fly from Africa to Europe each year.

In Saudi Arabia, you may see the plain tiger. It lays its eggs on a plant called ushar. The plant has a bitter juice. The young eat it, so birds do not like their taste.

versions.title: From Caterpillar to Butterfly
versions.text:
If you look closely under a green leaf, you might find a tiny round dot no bigger than a pin's head. It may be a butterfly egg. The mother chose that plant with care, because its leaves are the food her young will need.

When the egg hatches, a small caterpillar crawls out. Its first meal is often its own egg shell. Then it begins to munch on leaves, and it grows very fast. But a caterpillar's skin can not stretch much. When the skin gets too tight, the caterpillar sheds it. A new, larger skin is already waiting under it. A caterpillar does this four or five times.

Once it is fully grown, the caterpillar stops eating. It hangs from a stem and forms a hard case around its body. This case is called a chrysalis. Inside, an amazing change takes place. Most of the old body breaks down into a kind of soup! Then the parts of a brand-new body form. For many kinds of butterflies, this change takes about two weeks.

At last, the case splits open, and a butterfly climbs out. At first, its wings are wet and crumpled. The butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits for them to dry. Then it is ready to fly.

A butterfly can not chew. It sips sweet nectar from flowers through a long tube that works like a drinking straw. It can even taste with its feet! As it feeds, it carries pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

Some butterflies travel very far. Painted ladies fly between Africa and Europe each year.

In Saudi Arabia, you may spot the orange plain tiger. It lays its eggs on a plant called ushar, which has a bitter juice. The caterpillars eat the leaves, so birds do not like their taste.

versions.title: From Caterpillar to Butterfly
versions.text:
If you look closely under a green leaf, you might find a tiny round dot no bigger than a pin's head. It could be a butterfly egg. The female chose that plant with great care, because its leaves are the food her young will need.

When the egg hatches, a small caterpillar crawls out. Scientists call this stage the larva. Its first meal is often its own egg shell, and then it begins to gobble up leaves. The caterpillar grows very fast, but its skin cannot stretch much. When the skin gets too tight, the caterpillar splits it and wriggles out. This shedding is called a molt, and a larger skin is already waiting underneath. Most caterpillars molt four or five times.

Once the caterpillar is fully grown, it stops eating and hangs from a stem. It forms a hard case around its body, and this case is called a chrysalis. Scientists call this stage the pupa. Inside, a stunning change takes place. Most of the old body breaks down into a kind of soup! Then the parts of a whole new body form. For many butterflies, this change takes about two weeks.

At last, the chrysalis splits open, and the adult butterfly starts to emerge. At first, its wings are wet and crumpled. The butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits for them to dry before it flies.

A butterfly cannot chew. It drinks sweet nectar through a long, curled tube called a proboscis, which works like a drinking straw. It can even taste with its feet! As it feeds, it carries pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

Some butterflies travel huge distances. Painted ladies fly between Africa and Europe each year.

In Saudi Arabia, you may spot the orange plain tiger. It lays its eggs on a plant called ushar, which has a bitter, poisonous juice. The caterpillars eat the leaves, so birds learn to stay away from them because they taste so bad.

versions.title: The Amazing Life Cycle of a Butterfly
versions.text:
If you carefully examine the underside of a green leaf, you might discover a tiny spherical dot no larger than a pinhead. It could be a butterfly egg, and the female that deposited it selected that particular plant deliberately, because its leaves will provide the nourishment her offspring require to survive.

When the egg hatches, a small caterpillar crawls out, and scientists call this stage the larva. Its first meal is frequently its own egg shell, after which it begins devouring leaves continuously. Although the caterpillar grows remarkably fast, its skin cannot stretch very much. Whenever the skin becomes too tight, the caterpillar splits it open and wriggles out, revealing a larger skin that was already developing underneath. This shedding process is called a molt, and most caterpillars molt four or five times.

Once the caterpillar is fully grown, it stops eating and suspends itself from a stem. It then forms a hard protective case called a chrysalis, and scientists refer to this stage as the pupa. Inside, an astonishing transformation occurs. Most of the old body breaks down into a kind of soup, and then the structures of an entirely new body develop. For many species, this process requires approximately two weeks.

Eventually, the chrysalis splits open, and the adult butterfly begins to emerge. Initially, its wings are wet and crumpled, so the butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits for them to dry before it attempts to fly.

A butterfly cannot chew. Instead, it drinks sweet nectar through a long, coiled tube called a proboscis, which functions like a drinking straw. Remarkably, it can even taste with its feet. As it feeds, it transfers pollen between flowers, which helps plants produce seeds.

Some butterflies travel enormous distances. Painted ladies, for example, migrate between Africa and Europe annually.

In Saudi Arabia, you may notice the orange plain tiger. It deposits its eggs on a plant called ushar, which contains a bitter, poisonous juice. Because the caterpillars consume these leaves, birds learn to avoid them, since they taste terrible.

versions.title: Metamorphosis: The Butterfly's Great Change
versions.text:
If you carefully examine the underside of a green leaf, you might discover a tiny round dot no larger than a pinhead, and it could be a butterfly egg. The female that laid it chose that particular plant deliberately, because its leaves will provide the food her offspring need to survive.

When the egg hatches, a small caterpillar crawls out, and scientists call this stage the larva. Its first meal is frequently its own egg shell, after which it begins devouring leaves almost without stopping. Although the caterpillar grows remarkably fast, its skin cannot stretch very much, so whenever the skin becomes too tight, the caterpillar splits it open and wriggles out, revealing a larger skin that was already waiting underneath. This shedding process is called molting, and most caterpillars molt four or five times.

Once the caterpillar is fully grown, it stops eating and hangs from a stem, where it forms a hard protective case called a chrysalis, and scientists refer to this stage as the pupa. Inside, an astonishing transformation occurs, because most of the old body begins to dissolve into a kind of soup, and then the parts of an entirely new body develop. For many species this process takes about two weeks, and this complete change in form, from egg to larva to pupa to adult, is called metamorphosis.

Eventually, the chrysalis splits open, and the adult butterfly emerges. At first its wings are wet and crumpled, so the butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits for them to dry and harden before it attempts to fly.

A butterfly cannot chew, so it drinks sweet nectar through a long, coiled tube called a proboscis, which works like a drinking straw, and remarkably, it can even taste with its feet. As it feeds, it carries pollen between flowers, and in this way it helps to pollinate plants so that they can produce seeds.

Some butterflies travel enormous distances. Painted ladies, for example, make a migration between Africa and Europe every year.

In Saudi Arabia, you may notice the orange plain tiger, which lays its eggs on a plant called ushar that contains a bitter, poisonous juice. Because the caterpillars eat these leaves, birds and other predators learn to avoid them, since they taste terrible.

versions.title: Metamorphosis: The Butterfly's Great Change
versions.text:
If you carefully examine the underside of a green leaf, you might discover a tiny round dot no larger than a pinhead, and it could well be a butterfly egg. The female that deposited it selected that particular plant deliberately, because its leaves will provide the nourishment her offspring will require in order to survive.

Once the caterpillar is fully grown, it stops eating and suspends itself from a stem, where it forms a hard protective case called a chrysalis, and scientists refer to this stage as the pupa. Inside, an astonishing transformation occurs, because most of the old body tissue begins to dissolve into a kind of soup, after which the structures of an entirely new body develop. For many species, this process requires approximately two weeks. This complete change in form, from egg to larva to pupa to adult, is called metamorphosis.

Eventually, the chrysalis splits open and the adult butterfly emerges, but its wings are initially wet and crumpled, so the butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits for them to dry and harden before it attempts to fly.

As it feeds, it transfers pollen between flowers, and in this way it helps to pollinate plants so that they can produce seeds.

Some butterflies travel enormous distances, and painted ladies, for example, make a migration between Africa and Europe every year.

In Saudi Arabia, you may notice the orange plain tiger, which deposits its eggs on a plant called ushar that contains a bitter, poisonous juice. Because the caterpillars consume these leaves, birds and other predators learn to avoid them, since they taste terrible.

versions.title: Metamorphosis: The Butterfly's Great Change
versions.text:
If you carefully examine the underside of a green leaf, you might discover a tiny spherical dot no larger than a pinhead, and it could well be a butterfly egg. The female that deposited it selected that particular plant deliberately, because its leaves will provide the specific nourishment her offspring will require in order to survive.

When the egg hatches, a minuscule caterpillar emerges, and scientists classify this stage as the larva. Its first meal is frequently its own discarded egg shell, after which it begins devouring vegetation almost continuously. Although the caterpillar grows remarkably rapidly, its outer skin cannot stretch significantly, so whenever the skin becomes too tight, the caterpillar splits it open and wriggles free, revealing a larger skin that was already developing underneath. This shedding process is called molting, and most caterpillars molt four or five times before they reach their full size.

Once the caterpillar is fully grown, it stops eating and suspends itself from a stem, where it forms a hard protective case called a chrysalis, and scientists refer to this stage as the pupa. Inside, an astonishing transformation occurs, because most of the old body tissue begins to dissolve into a kind of soup, after which the structures of an entirely new body gradually develop. For many species this process requires approximately two weeks, and this complete change in form, from egg to larva to pupa to adult, is known as metamorphosis.

Eventually, the chrysalis splits open and the adult butterfly emerges, but its wings are initially damp and crumpled, so the butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits patiently for them to dry and harden before it attempts to fly.

A butterfly cannot chew, so instead it drinks sugary nectar through a long, coiled tube called a proboscis, which functions like a drinking straw, and remarkably, it can even taste with its feet. As it feeds, it transfers pollen between flowers, and in this way it helps to pollinate plants so that they can produce seeds.

Some butterflies travel extraordinary distances, and painted ladies, for example, complete an annual migration between Africa and Europe.

In Saudi Arabia, observant people may notice the orange plain tiger, which deposits its eggs on a plant called ushar that contains a bitter, poisonous juice. Because the caterpillars consume these leaves, birds and other predators learn to avoid them, since they taste terrible.

versions.title: Metamorphosis: The Butterfly's Great Change
versions.text:
If you carefully examine the underside of a green leaf, you might discover a tiny spherical dot no larger than a pinhead, and it could very well be a butterfly egg. The female that deposited it selected that particular plant deliberately, because its foliage will provide the specific nourishment her offspring will require in order to survive.

When the egg hatches, a minuscule caterpillar emerges, and entomologists classify this developmental stage as the larva. Its first meal is frequently its own discarded egg shell, after which it begins consuming vegetation almost continuously. Although the caterpillar grows extraordinarily rapidly, its outer skin cannot stretch significantly, so whenever the skin becomes uncomfortably tight, the caterpillar splits it open and wriggles free, revealing a more spacious skin that was already developing underneath. This shedding process is called molting, and most caterpillars molt four or five times before they reach their maximum size.

Once the caterpillar is fully grown, it stops eating and suspends itself from a stem, where it constructs a hard protective case called a chrysalis, and scientists refer to this stage as the pupa. Inside, an astonishing transformation occurs, because most of the original body tissue begins to dissolve into a kind of nutritious soup, after which the structures of an entirely new body gradually develop. For many species this reorganization requires approximately two weeks, and this complete alteration in form, from egg to larva to pupa to adult, is known as metamorphosis.

Eventually, the chrysalis splits open and the adult butterfly emerges, but its wings are initially damp and crumpled, so the butterfly pumps fluid into them and waits patiently for them to dry and harden before it attempts its first flight.

A butterfly is incapable of chewing, so instead it drinks sugary nectar through a long, coiled tube called a proboscis, which functions like a drinking straw, and remarkably, it can even detect flavors with its feet. As it feeds, it transfers pollen between flowers, and in this way it helps to pollinate numerous plants so that they can produce seeds.

Some butterflies travel extraordinary distances, and painted ladies, for example, complete an annual migration between Africa and Europe.

In Saudi Arabia, observant naturalists may notice the orange plain tiger, which deposits its eggs on a plant called ushar that contains a bitter, poisonous substance. Because the caterpillars consume these leaves, birds and other predators learn to avoid them, since they taste extremely unpleasant.

versions.title: Metamorphosis: The Butterfly's Great Change
versions.text:
A butterfly's life begins not as a miniature version of its adult self but as something almost unrecognizable: a single egg, laid with deliberate care by a female on a plant her offspring will need to survive. When the larva emerges, its first meal is often the egg shell itself, a source of nutrients before it turns to the leaves around it. As a caterpillar, it does little but eat, and because its exoskeleton cannot expand indefinitely, it must periodically shed this rigid outer layer in a process called molting, repeating the sequence four or five times as it grows.

Eventually the caterpillar undergoes metamorphosis, the dramatic transformation that distinguishes butterflies from animals that simply grow larger without changing shape. It forms a hardened case known as a chrysalis, and within this seemingly motionless shell an astonishing process unfolds: the caterpillar's body does not merely rearrange itself but largely dissolves into a soft, soupy mixture from which entirely new structures, including wings, legs, and antennae, are gradually built. This reconstruction typically requires about two weeks, though the exact duration depends on temperature and species.

When the adult finally emerges, its body bears little resemblance to the creature that entered the chrysalis. It possesses a long, coiled feeding tube called a proboscis, uncurled to draw nectar from flowers, and strangely, it tastes its food not with a tongue but through sensory receptors in its feet. As it moves from blossom to blossom, pollen clings to its body and is carried to other flowers, making the butterfly an unintentional but essential pollinator for many plants.

Not all butterflies remain in one place. Painted lady butterflies undertake a remarkable annual migration between Africa and Europe, traveling vast distances that no single generation completes alone; later generations continue the journey their ancestors began. In Saudi Arabia, the plain tiger butterfly lays its eggs on the ushar plant, a species whose sap is bitter and even poisonous. Caterpillars that feed on it absorb these toxins into their own tissues, becoming distasteful or harmful to predators that might otherwise eat them, a defense that persists into adulthood.

Every stage of this cycle, from egg to larva to pupa to adult, serves a distinct purpose, and the chrysalis stage in particular demonstrates how dramatically an organism can be rebuilt from within while remaining, in essence, the same individual.

None of this would be possible without the predator pressures that have shaped butterfly biology over countless generations. A caterpillar that tastes bitter to a hungry bird survives to complete metamorphosis, while one lacking such defenses rarely does, and this simple pressure explains why the plain tiger caterpillar's reliance on the toxic ushar plant persists generation after generation in the deserts of Saudi Arabia. The same logic underlies the painted lady's migration: a butterfly that follows favorable seasonal conditions between Africa and Europe gains access to food and breeding sites unavailable to one that remains in a single location year-round.

versions.title: Metamorphosis: The Butterfly's Great Change
versions.text:
The life cycle of a butterfly unfolds through a sequence of stages so distinct from one another that an observer unfamiliar with insects might assume each represented an entirely different species. It begins when a female deposits an egg upon a specific host plant, chosen because it will later provide sustenance for her offspring. Upon hatching, the emerging larva typically consumes the remains of its own egg shell before turning to the surrounding foliage, and because its rigid exoskeleton cannot accommodate continuous growth, the caterpillar must molt repeatedly, shedding its outer covering four or five times across its development.

The most extraordinary phase, however, is metamorphosis itself, the process that transforms a crawling, leaf-eating larva into a winged, nectar-feeding adult. Encased within a protective chrysalis, the caterpillar's body undergoes a transformation so thorough that its internal structures largely dissolve into an amorphous, soup-like substance, from which the wings, legs, antennae, and other organs of the adult butterfly are subsequently assembled. This reorganization, requiring roughly two weeks under typical conditions, represents one of the most profound structural transformations found anywhere in the animal kingdom, since few other organisms discard so much of their prior architecture while continuing to exist as the same living individual.

Once emerged, the adult butterfly is equipped with specialized anatomy unlike anything possessed at earlier stages: a slender, coiled proboscis that unfurls to probe deep into flowers for nectar, and sensory receptors located in its feet that allow it to taste potential food sources before ever extending its mouthparts. As the insect travels between blossoms in search of nourishment, pollen grains adhere to its body and are inadvertently transported from flower to flower, rendering the butterfly a significant, if unintentional, agent of pollination within its ecosystem.

Migration further complicates the simple image of a short-lived insect confined to a single habitat. Painted lady butterflies, for instance, undertake an extensive annual migration spanning Africa and Europe, a journey so long that no individual butterfly completes it alone; instead, successive generations relay the route, each contributing a portion before giving way to its descendants. In the arid landscapes of Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, the plain tiger butterfly selects the ushar plant as its preferred host despite the plant's bitter, toxic sap. Caterpillars that feed upon it incorporate these compounds into their own tissues, acquiring a chemical defense that renders them unpalatable or outright harmful to predators, a protection that persists well after metamorphosis into adulthood.

Taken together, the egg, larva, pupa, and adult stages illustrate a biological strategy in which vulnerability at one phase of life is offset by specialized defenses, mobility, or ecological utility at another, with metamorphosis serving as the pivotal mechanism that connects these otherwise disparate forms into a single, continuous life history.

None of this intricate life history would be possible without the sustained predator pressures that have shaped butterfly biology across countless successive generations. A caterpillar whose tissues taste bitter or toxic to a hungry bird is considerably more likely to survive long enough to complete metamorphosis, whereas one lacking such chemical defenses rarely does, and this straightforward evolutionary pressure explains why the plain tiger caterpillar's dependence upon the toxic ushar plant persists generation after generation throughout the deserts of Saudi Arabia. An identical underlying logic governs the painted lady's extensive migration: a butterfly population that follows favorable seasonal conditions between Africa and Europe gains access to food sources and breeding sites unavailable to populations that remain confined to a single location throughout the year, a pattern repeated with remarkable consistency across successive migratory generations.

keyWords.definition: a young butterfly or moth that looks like a soft worm and eats leaves

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?

How a caterpillar changes into a butterfly
Why birds eat caterpillars
How plants make sweet nectar
questions.why: The whole article follows one animal from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly.

wrong.A: The article never tells how to catch butterflies.
wrong.C: Birds are named near the end, but they are not the main topic.
wrong.D: Nectar is named, but the article does not explain how plants make it.

Sweet nectar

wrong.B: Pollen is moved by the adult butterfly, not eaten by the caterpillar.
wrong.D: Nectar is what the adult butterfly drinks, not the caterpillar's first meal.

About ten times
It never sheds its skin

As a list of problems and fixes
In the order of a butterfly's life
From the biggest bug to the smallest
questions.why: The article starts with the egg, then the caterpillar, the case, and the grown butterfly, in the order they happen.

wrong.A: Bees are not in the article.
wrong.B: The article does not list problems and fixes.
wrong.D: The article does not compare bugs by size.

LOW.prompt: Tell the four stages of a butterfly's life in order. Write one thing that happens in each stage.
checklist: I named all four stages in the right order.
I wrote one true fact from the article for each stage.
I used at least two key words, such as chrysalis or nectar.
LOW.modelAnswer: First is the egg, a tiny dot on a leaf. Next, a caterpillar hatches out and eats leaves to grow bigger. Then it forms a hard chrysalis and changes inside. Last, it becomes an adult butterfly that drinks nectar from flowers.

keyWords.definition: the young, worm-like stage of an insect, such as a caterpillar
keyWords.example: The beetle larva lived under the log and ate rotting wood.

keyWords.definition: to shed an old outer skin so a bigger one can take its place
keyWords.example: Snakes molt and leave their old skins behind on the rocks.

keyWords.definition: the resting stage of an insect when it changes into an adult
keyWords.example: The pupa stayed still for days while the change took place.

keyWords.definition: a long, thin mouth part that some insects use to suck up liquid
keyWords.example: The moth uncurled its proboscis to reach deep into the flower.

keyWords.definition: to come out from inside or behind something
keyWords.example: The sun began to emerge from behind the clouds.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: A butterfly goes through four stages and changes its whole body as it grows.
Caterpillars eat more leaves than any other animal on Earth.
Butterflies need real straws to drink their food from flowers.
Painted ladies are the strongest butterflies in the world.
questions.why: Every part of the article follows the butterfly through the egg, larva, pupa, and adult stages and explains the big change in its body.

wrong.B: The article says caterpillars eat a lot, but it never compares them with every other animal.
wrong.C: The straw is a comparison for the proboscis, not something butterflies really use.
wrong.D: The article says painted ladies travel far, not that they are the strongest.

questions.stem: What do scientists call the stage when the caterpillar is inside the chrysalis?
options: The larva
The molt
The pupa
The adult
questions.why: The article says the caterpillar forms a chrysalis, and scientists call this stage the pupa.

wrong.A: The larva is the caterpillar stage, before the chrysalis.
wrong.B: A molt is the shedding of skin, not a stage.
wrong.D: The adult is the butterfly that comes out at the end.

questions.stem: As it is used in the article, what does molt mean?
options: To munch on a leaf
To shed an old skin
To fly a long way
To hang from a stem
questions.why: The article says the caterpillar splits its tight skin and wriggles out, and this shedding is called a molt.

wrong.A: Eating leaves is how it grows, not what molt means.
wrong.C: Flying far is how the article describes painted ladies.
wrong.D: Hanging from a stem happens before the pupa stage, not during a molt.

questions.stem: How does a butterfly drink nectar?
options: It chews the petals of a flower.
It licks the nectar with its feet.
It soaks it up through its wings.
It sips it up through a proboscis.
questions.why: The article says the butterfly cannot chew, so it drinks nectar through a long, curled tube called a proboscis.

wrong.A: The article says a butterfly cannot chew.
wrong.B: The butterfly can taste with its feet, but it does not drink with them.
wrong.C: The article says nothing about wings soaking up food.

questions.stem: Why does a caterpillar need to molt?
options: Its skin cannot stretch much as it grows.
It wants to change the color of its body.
Its old skin slowly becomes poisonous.
Birds keep pulling bits of its skin off.
questions.why: The article explains that the caterpillar grows fast but its skin cannot stretch much, so when the skin gets too tight, it sheds it.

wrong.B: The article does not connect molting with color.
wrong.C: The poison in the article comes from the ushar plant, not old skin.
wrong.D: The article does not say birds pull off the skin.

questions.stem: What can you infer about a bird that has already tasted a plain tiger caterpillar?
options: It will look for more of them.
It will feed them to its young.
It will probably not eat another one.
It will start eating ushar leaves.
questions.why: The caterpillars taste bad because they eat the poisonous ushar plant, and the article says birds learn to avoid them. So one bad taste teaches the bird.

wrong.A: A bird would not look for food that tasted bad.
wrong.B: The article gives no reason to feed something bad-tasting to young birds.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests the bird would start eating the plant.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a butterfly laid its eggs on a plant its caterpillars cannot eat?
options: The caterpillars would molt faster.
The caterpillars would not have the food they need.
The eggs would hatch into adults.
The plant would make more nectar.
questions.why: The article says the female chooses the plant because its leaves are the food her young will need. On the wrong plant, the young would have nothing to eat.

wrong.A: Without food, a caterpillar could not grow, so it would not molt faster.
wrong.C: Eggs always hatch into caterpillars first, never straight into adults.
wrong.D: The article does not connect egg-laying with nectar.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the paragraph about Saudi Arabia?
options: To prove that butterflies live only in Saudi Arabia
To explain how painted ladies migrate
To list every butterfly that lives in the desert
To show a local butterfly whose food plant helps keep it safe
questions.why: The paragraph describes the plain tiger, which lays eggs on ushar, and explains how the bitter plant makes its caterpillars taste bad to birds.

wrong.A: The article shows butterflies in many places, including Africa and Europe.
wrong.B: Painted ladies are in a different paragraph.
wrong.C: The paragraph names only one butterfly.

MID.prompt: Explain what happens inside the chrysalis. Why do you think scientists find this stage so amazing?
checklist: I explained that the old body breaks down and a new body forms.
I gave a reason, using details from the article.
I used the words pupa or emerge correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Inside the chrysalis, which is the pupa stage, most of the caterpillar's old body breaks down into a kind of soup, and then an entirely new body gradually develops from it. I think scientists find this stage so amazing because the article says this whole transformation takes about two weeks, and when the adult butterfly finally starts to emerge, it looks nothing like the caterpillar that went in. It is incredible that a creature can rebuild its entire body in such a short time.

keyWords.definition: a complete change in the form of an animal as it grows into an adult
keyWords.example: A frog goes through metamorphosis, starting life as a tadpole with a tail.

keyWords.definition: to break down until it mixes into a liquid
keyWords.example: Stir the water so the sugar will dissolve quickly.

keyWords.definition: to carry pollen from one flower to another so the plant can make seeds
keyWords.example: Farmers keep bees near their orchards to pollinate the trees.

keyWords.definition: a long journey that animals make from one region to another, often each year
keyWords.example: The migration of storks takes them across deserts and seas.

keyWords.definition: an animal that hunts and eats other animals
keyWords.example: The fox is a predator that hunts rabbits at night.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Butterflies are the most important pollinators on Earth.
Caterpillars are pests that farmers must control.
A butterfly's life is a complete change in form, from egg to larva to pupa to adult.
Painted ladies and plain tigers are the only butterflies in Arabia.
questions.why: The article traces every stage of the butterfly's life and names this complete change metamorphosis.

wrong.A: The article says butterflies help pollinate plants, but it does not rank them against other pollinators.
wrong.B: The article never calls caterpillars pests.
wrong.D: The article names these two butterflies as examples, not as the only ones.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to most of the caterpillar's body inside the chrysalis?
options: It dissolves into a kind of soup before a new body develops.
It hardens into a thick shell that later cracks open.
It stays the same but grows a pair of wings.
It shrinks until it can fit inside the egg again.
questions.why: The article says most of the old body tissue begins to dissolve into a kind of soup, after which the structures of a new body develop.

wrong.B: The chrysalis is the hard case, but the body inside does not harden.
wrong.C: The article stresses that the body changes completely, not that it stays the same.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article says the body returns to the egg.

questions.stem: In the article, what does it mean that butterflies help to pollinate plants?
options: They eat harmful insects on the plants.
They protect the plants from predators.
They lay eggs that feed the plants.
They carry pollen from flower to flower.
questions.why: The article says that as a butterfly feeds, it transfers pollen between flowers, and in this way it helps to pollinate plants so that they can produce seeds.

wrong.A: The article does not say butterflies eat insects.
wrong.B: Protection from predators is about the caterpillars, not the plants.
wrong.C: Butterfly eggs become caterpillars that eat plants; they do not feed them.

questions.stem: Which journey does the article describe as an annual migration?
options: Plain tigers flying across the Arabian desert
Painted ladies traveling between Africa and Europe
Caterpillars crawling from one plant to another
Butterflies returning to the plant where they hatched
questions.why: The article states that painted ladies complete an annual migration between Africa and Europe.

wrong.A: The plain tiger is described with the ushar plant, not with a migration.
wrong.C: Crawling between plants is not described as a migration.
wrong.D: The article never says butterflies return to where they hatched.

questions.stem: Why do birds and other predators learn to avoid plain tiger caterpillars?
options: The caterpillars hide inside a hard chrysalis all their lives.
The caterpillars are too small to be worth eating.
The caterpillars eat ushar, a plant with a bitter poison, so they taste unpleasant.
The caterpillars sting predators with their feet.
questions.why: The article explains that because the caterpillars consume ushar leaves, which contain a bitter, poisonous substance, predators learn to avoid them.

wrong.A: The chrysalis is only one stage, not the whole life.
wrong.B: Size is not given as the reason.
wrong.D: The article says butterflies taste with their feet, not sting with them.

questions.stem: Which list shows the stages of metamorphosis in the correct order?
options: Egg, larva, pupa, adult
Larva, egg, adult, pupa
Egg, pupa, larva, adult
Pupa, larva, egg, adult
questions.why: The article names the complete change in form as going from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

wrong.B: The egg must come first, before the larva.
wrong.C: The larva (caterpillar) comes before the pupa (chrysalis).
wrong.D: The pupa cannot come first; it forms only after the larva is fully grown.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a butterfly tried to fly the moment it left the chrysalis?
options: It would fly faster than an older butterfly.
It would need to molt one more time first.
It would return to being a caterpillar.
Its wet wings could not carry it well.
questions.why: The article says the new wings are damp and crumpled and must be filled with fluid, then dry and harden, before the first flight. Flying sooner would likely fail.

wrong.A: The article gives no reason a new butterfly would be faster.
wrong.B: Molting happens only in the caterpillar stage.
wrong.C: Metamorphosis goes one way; the article never says it can reverse.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a butterfly's proboscis to a drinking straw?
options: To prove that butterflies can drink any liquid
To help readers picture how the butterfly sucks up nectar
To show that people invented the straw by copying butterflies
To explain why butterflies cannot taste their food
questions.why: Comparing an unfamiliar body part to a familiar object helps readers imagine how the long, coiled tube draws up nectar.

wrong.A: The article only mentions nectar, not every kind of liquid.
wrong.C: The article says nothing about how straws were invented.
wrong.D: The article says butterflies can even taste with their feet.

HIGH.prompt: The article calls the change inside the chrysalis an astonishing transformation. Do you agree? Support your answer with at least two details from the article.
checklist: I stated whether I agree and explained why.
I used at least two accurate details from the article.
I used the words metamorphosis and dissolve correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that the change inside the chrysalis is an astonishing metamorphosis. According to the article, most of the caterpillar's old body actually seems to dissolve into a kind of soup before the parts of an entirely new body develop in its place, which is a far more dramatic change than simply growing bigger. It is also remarkable that this complete rebuilding happens in only about two weeks, turning a leaf-eating caterpillar into a winged adult that drinks nectar through a proboscis, a transformation almost nothing else in nature can match.
